caption:
For the next 9 weeks I'm sharing the complete methodology from Process Kaizen — chapter by chapter, twice a day, in order.

This is the same playbook I use on every consulting engagement. Forty-five days from now, you'll have the full toolkit for running a Kaizen Event from charter to control plan.

If you've ever wondered why most process improvement work doesn't stick — this is going to be useful.

First topic: what a Kaizen Event actually is, and why the format matters more than the tools.

Kaizen is Japanese for gradual, unending improvement.

A Kaizen Event is the structured way to do it: five focused days, the right people in the room, a single process targeted for change, and implemented improvements demonstrated by Friday.

It's not a workshop. Workshops produce reports.
It's not a brainstorm. Brainstorms produce ideas.
It's an event — with a charter, a baseline, a measurement system, and a control plan.

The format is what makes it work.

Six principles hold every Lean system together:

1. Specify value from the customer's perspective
2. Identify the value stream and eliminate the waste in it
3. Make the value-creating steps flow
4. Let the customer pull value through the process
5. Pursue perfection
6. Respect every person involved in the work

Notice what's not on this list: tools.

Tools come last. These principles come first — and they're what separates a Lean transformation from a flavor-of-the-month initiative.

Lean Thinking is a methodology, not a toolkit.

It came out of postwar Toyota and was formalized in the West in the 1990s. The core insight: most of what happens in any process doesn't add value to the customer.

In a typical office process, 98% of cycle time is lag. Queues. Approvals. Outboxes. Handoffs. Only about 2% is actual work.

Once you see this ratio, you can't unsee it. And it changes how you measure everything.

Six Sigma is the statistical sibling of Lean.

Where Lean focuses on eliminating waste, Six Sigma focuses on eliminating variation. The two are complementary, and most modern practice (Lean Six Sigma) uses both.

The vocabulary you'll hear over the next several weeks: DMAIC. Sigma levels. DPMO. Cause and Effect Matrix. FMEA. Risk Priority Number.

Each one will be explained in plain English. No statistics degree required.

6S is where most Lean programs start. And where many programs fail to start.

Sort. Set in Order. Shine. Standardize. Sustain. Safety.

It looks like housekeeping. It is housekeeping. But it's also the foundation that makes everything else visible — waste, defects, near-misses, drift.

You can't improve a process you can't see clearly. 6S makes the process visible. Everything in the rest of the book depends on it.

Visual Controls let anyone — including a visitor walking through — understand the current state of a process at a glance.

Kanban is the most famous example: a card or signal that says when to produce, withdraw, or replenish.

Both rest on the same principle: information lives where the work happens. Not in a dashboard nobody opens. Not in a meeting once a month.

At the point of work. At the moment it's needed.

Push: "We made it, here it is, deal with it."
Pull: "The customer asked, so we made it."

Push systems accumulate inventory, hide problems, and reward overproduction. Pull systems force the upstream to listen to the downstream.

One-piece flow is pull taken to its logical end. Batch size of one. Each unit moves through the process individually. Problems surface in seconds, not in next quarter's audit.

DMAIC is the project structure for every Kaizen Event:

Define — scope and charter
Measure — size the current state
Analyze — find the few critical inputs
Improve — implement and demonstrate
Control — sustain the gains

The seven chapters of Process Kaizen map directly to this. Most failures happen because teams skip a phase — usually Define or Control. Don't.

The discipline is what makes the methodology work.

A 5-day Kaizen Event has three parts:

Days 1-2: Define and Measure. Map the process. Size the waste. Build consensus on the current state.

Days 3-4: Analyze and Improve. Find the critical inputs. Implement the fixes.

Day 5: Demonstrate. Show the work to the sponsor. Sign the Control Plan.

If you can't get the right people for five focused days, you're not running an event. You're running a workshop.

Chapter 1 is the question most teams skip: should we even be running an event on this process?

Most Kaizen Events fail not because of poor execution, but because they were chartered against the wrong process.

The next seven posts cover Chapter 1: Identify Opportunity. Strategic goals. Baseline data. Stakeholder needs. Variance analysis. Organizational assessments. Prioritization.

Skip this work and you'll run a perfect event on a process that didn't matter.

There are five ways an improvement opportunity enters the Kaizen funnel:

1. Strategic goals (top-down direction)
2. Variance to plan (performance gaps)
3. Stakeholder ideas (bottom-up signals)
4. Organizational assessments (formal reviews)
5. Baseline performance data (the numbers)

The trap is overweighting #1. Top-down goals matter — but the best Kaizen opportunities almost always come from the floor, where the actual work happens.

Build a system that captures all five.

Before you can improve a process, you have to know what you're measuring.

Activity 1.02 names the measurement: what number defines success? Cycle time? Defect rate? Cost per unit? On-time delivery?

Then it captures the baseline. Real numbers from the current state. Not estimates. Not "about a month." Actual data, with sample size.

Without a baseline, you can't prove the improvement. Without proof, the gains drift away within six months.

The Andon Cord is the original variance signal.

On a Toyota assembly line, any operator can pull a cord that stops the line when something is wrong. The cord triggers immediate response — not a meeting next quarter.

Your organization's equivalent: any reliable system that surfaces variance from plan within hours, not months.

If your variance signals take 30 days to reach someone with authority to act, your improvement system is broken before it starts.

The Idea Board is where bottom-up improvement starts.

A physical or digital board where any team member can submit an observation: "this step takes too long," "this form is unclear," "this handoff drops 15% of the time."

Most organizations have a suggestion box that nobody opens. The Idea Board is different — every item gets reviewed, scored, and either accepted into the backlog or explained back to the submitter.

Closed-loop matters. People stop submitting when they stop getting answers.

The Organizational Assessment is the formal version of "what are we bad at?"

A structured review of process capability across the organization. Could be a quarterly leadership exercise. Could be an annual maturity assessment.

What matters: it produces a ranked list of process pain points, scored against strategic priority and current performance gap.

That ranked list feeds the Kaizen pipeline. Without it, charter decisions get made on whoever shouts loudest in the room.

Baseline performance is the line you'll draw the improvement against.

Three rules for a usable baseline:

1. It comes from observation, not memory. Time the work.
2. It has sample size. One data point is an anecdote.
3. It's documented before the event starts, not reconstructed after.

The single most common reason post-Kaizen improvements get challenged: nobody trusts the baseline. Build it carefully.

You can't run a Kaizen Event on every opportunity. You need a filter.

Three filters for prioritizing:

1. Strategic alignment — does this serve the organization's stated direction?
2. Process capability — is the process broken enough that an event will move the needle?
3. Team readiness — are the right people available for five days?

If a candidate process fails any filter, it doesn't get chartered. Park it. Come back to it when the conditions change.

Chapter 2 is where the project charter gets written.

Six activities take you from "this process is broken" to "here's what we'll do about it, who's responsible, and what success looks like."

Most teams skip this work and dive straight into the event. They show up Day 1 without a clear problem statement, without a financial impact estimate, without sponsor commitment. By Wednesday they're arguing about scope.

Charter the project. Then run the event.

Activity 2.01: take the baseline from Chapter 1 and stress-test it.

Five questions:
- Where did this number come from?
- How recent is the data?
- What's the sample size?
- Is the measurement system reliable?
- Would the process owner agree with it?

If any of those answers is shaky, the baseline isn't ready. Fix it before you write the charter. A charter built on a wobbly baseline gets challenged at every milestone.

Hard savings hit the P&L. Soft savings don't.

Hard savings: reduced labor cost, lower scrap, reduced overtime, eliminated outside spend.

Soft savings: hours saved per week, reduced cycle time, fewer escalations.

Both matter. But your sponsor cares about hard savings — they fund engagements. Build your charter financial case around hard. Mention soft as supporting context.

If you can't articulate the hard dollar impact, the engagement isn't ready to start.

A good Kaizen objective is specific, measurable, and time-bound.

Bad: "Improve the onboarding process."
Good: "Reduce average customer onboarding time from 14 days to 7 days by end of Q3."

Bad: "Reduce defects."
Good: "Reduce KYC verification errors from 6% to under 1.5% within 90 days post-event."

The objective should be testable from a single number, measured the same way before and after. If two people can disagree on whether you hit the target, the objective is too vague.

Process Capability tells you whether the current process can ever meet the target.

Four conditions:
- Capable and stable: in control, hitting spec
- Capable but unstable: needs control discipline
- Stable but not capable: needs redesign
- Neither: needs both

A Kaizen Event works best in two of the four: capable-but-unstable and stable-but-not-capable. The other two need different interventions.

Diagnose before you charter.

A Kaizen Charter is a one-page contract between sponsor, team, and the organization.

Eight components:
1. Process name and scope (start point, end point)
2. Problem statement
3. Baseline performance
4. Target performance
5. Hard dollar impact
6. Project team and sponsor
7. Event dates
8. Out-of-scope items (just as important)

If the charter doesn't fit on one page, the scope is too big. Cut it before you start.

Once you have multiple charters in the pipeline, you need a way to rank them.

Score each charter on:
- Strategic alignment (1-10)
- Financial impact (in dollars)
- Implementation ease (1-10, higher = easier)
- Team availability (1-10)

Sort by financial impact × strategic alignment × ease. The top three are your next quarter's events.

This is the same prioritization logic you'll apply inside an event — to inputs, to backlog items, to actions. Build the muscle.

Chapter 3 is project kickoff: getting from "we have a charter" to "we have a team ready to run on Monday."

Five activities:
- Identify the resources you need
- Schedule them
- Pre-load the data for analysis
- Run a Lean thinking exercise to align the team
- Walk through the charter together

Kickoff feels administrative. It's the highest-leverage week of the engagement. The right people, prepared, beats the wrong people, scrambling.

Five resource categories for any Kaizen Event:

1. People — the project team, sponsor, process owner, facilitator
2. Time — five days, blocked on calendars, no exceptions
3. Space — a dedicated room with wall space for visuals
4. Data — current state metrics, defect logs, process maps if any
5. Tools — whiteboards, sticky notes, the templates from this book

Most events go sideways because of resource #2 — calendar conflicts mid-week. Block the time first. Argue about everything else later.

Scheduling a Kaizen Event is not the same as scheduling a meeting.

You need five consecutive business days, all key participants for at least 80% of the time, executive sponsor for the Day 5 demo, and a process owner with decision authority in the room.

If any of those are missing, reschedule. A weakened lineup produces a weakened result — and the weakened result becomes the case study against running another event.

Before the event starts, the facilitator and process owner deep-dive the available data.

What's available: defect logs, cycle time samples, customer complaints, audit findings, prior process maps.

What you're looking for: the prior failure modes. Where has this process broken before? What workarounds emerged? Which steps does the team complain about most?

This deep dive becomes the first pass at the FMEA. Walk in informed, not blind.

Day 1 of every Kaizen Event opens with a Lean thinking exercise — a 90-minute simulation where the team experiences batch-and-queue, then experiences one-piece flow, then debriefs the difference.

It's not optional. The exercise establishes shared vocabulary and shared experience. Without it, half the team is operating on different mental models for the rest of the week.

You can't teach Lean in a slide deck. You have to make people feel the waste.

Before the work starts, the team reviews the charter together.

Three questions to ask:
- Does anyone disagree with the problem statement?
- Does anyone think the baseline is wrong?
- Does anyone think the target is unrealistic?

Surface disagreement now. The most common Kaizen failure is unspoken misalignment that surfaces on Thursday and torches the event.

If everyone says yes, you start. If anyone says no, you fix the charter before Day 1.

Chapter 4 is the Define phase: build a shared, accurate picture of how the process actually works today.

Seven activities take the team from a one-line problem statement to a fully mapped process, validated against reality.

Most teams skip the rigor here. They sketch a process flow in 30 minutes and start optimizing. By Wednesday they realize they were optimizing the wrong process.

Slow down in Define. The speed in Improve depends on it.

SIPOC is five columns:

Suppliers · Inputs · Process · Outputs · Customers

It takes 45 minutes to build. Most teams skip it because it looks too simple.

Then halfway through Day 2 they realize they've been mapping the wrong process, or they disagree on where the process starts, or they forgot a major customer.

Do SIPOC first. Every time. The simplicity is the point.

Five rules for building a useful SIPOC:

1. Start with Outputs and Customers. Work backward from what the process delivers.
2. List Inputs by category — material, information, decisions, signals.
3. Identify Suppliers for each Input, internal or external.
4. Process in this column is high-level. 4-8 steps maximum. No detail yet.
5. Build it on the wall, not in a doc. The team needs to point at it.

A good SIPOC is the foundation for every map that follows.

There are five levels of process detail. Each one is useful for a different conversation.

Level 1: SIPOC view — 4-8 boxes
Level 2: Cross-functional swim lanes — 15-30 steps
Level 3: Detailed activity flow — 50+ steps
Level 4: Value stream map — flow plus inventory and time
Level 5: Standard work — task-level instructions

The most common mistake: mapping at the wrong level for the decision you're trying to make. Match the level to the question.

The Level 1 Process Map is your team's shared model of how the process works.

Build it in this order:
1. Identify the trigger event — what starts the process?
2. Identify the end event — when is the process complete?
3. List the 4-8 major steps between
4. Identify hand-offs between functions
5. Mark decision points

If the team can't agree on the Level 1 map, you have a bigger problem than process inefficiency. You have organizational misalignment. Surface it now.

After Level 1, you go a layer deeper. Each major Level 1 box becomes its own Level 2 sub-process map.

This is where the workarounds surface. The sub-process is where senior team members say things like, "oh, we usually skip that step," or "that approval only happens half the time."

Capture all of it. The map you build here is the map you'll measure in Chapter 5 and analyze in Chapter 6. Inaccuracy compounds.

Before the team moves to Measure, the maps get one final pass:

1. Validate with two people who weren't in the room.
2. Walk through every step verbally — does it match how the work actually happens?
3. Mark steps where the team disagreed during construction.
4. Note any steps that nobody could explain — those are red flags.

A finalized Define-phase map is a contract. The rest of the week's analysis depends on it being right.

The Process Definition Document is the written companion to the maps.

It captures:
- The purpose of the process (one sentence)
- Inputs and outputs at each step
- Roles and responsibilities
- Tools and systems used
- Critical inputs flagged for deep analysis

It's the document the Process Owner refers to after the event. The maps tell you what the process looks like. The PDD tells you what each step is supposed to do.

Chapter 5 is Measure. Eight activities that size the current state numerically.

This is where most teams discover that the process they thought was "inefficient" is actually 98% waste.

You can't fix what you can't measure. And measurement in a Kaizen Event isn't a spreadsheet exercise — it's deliberately observed cycle times, classified work, and a value-added flow analysis that makes the waste visible.

source: 5.01 Establish Process Times and Lag Times
caption:
Two times matter in any process:

Process time — how long the work actually takes when someone is doing it.
Lag time — how long the work sits between steps, waiting.

The ratio tells you everything.

Manufacturing process: maybe 70% process, 30% lag.
Office process: typically 2% process, 98% lag.
Sales process: often 1% process, 99% lag.

Measure both. The gap is where the improvement opportunity lives.

Every process has one primary metric. The one number that, if it moves the right direction, the process is winning.

Pick yours carefully:
- Customer-facing? Use cycle time or on-time delivery.
- Quality-driven? Use defect rate or first-pass yield.
- Cost-driven? Use cost per unit or labor minutes per output.

One number. The rest are secondary metrics — they support the primary, they don't compete with it. Avoid metric proliferation. It dilutes accountability.

Once you have Level 1 times, you go deeper. Each sub-process gets timed.

Two methods:
- Direct observation. Stand next to the work, stopwatch in hand. Time it 5-10 times.
- Historical data extraction. Pull timestamps from systems where available.

Direct observation is slower but more accurate — it catches the actual work, including the workarounds. Historical data catches scale but misses the human reality. Use both.

Sub-processes have their own primary metrics, rolling up to the Level 1 primary.

The math has to add up. If the Level 1 primary is "cycle time under 24 hours," the sub-process metrics need to allocate that 24 hours across steps with realistic targets.

If your sub-process metrics sum to a number that doesn't match the Level 1 target, one of two things is true: the Level 1 target is wrong, or the sub-process allocation is wrong. Find out which.

The Eight Wastes — DOWNTIME, in English:

Defects · Overproduction · Waiting · Non-utilized talent · Transport · Inventory · Motion · Excess processing

Every step in your process gets classified as one of three: value-added (the customer would pay for it), business-value-added (required but not customer-valued), or non-value-added (waste, eliminate it).

Most teams discover that 30-70% of their steps fall into the third category. That's the improvement opportunity.

A Value-Added Flow Analysis classifies every step in your process.

For each step, ask:
- Does the customer care about this step? (Value-added)
- Is this required by regulation, policy, or system constraint? (Business-value-added)
- Is this neither? (Waste)

Color-code the map. Green for value-added, yellow for business-value, red for waste. The amount of red on the map is your visible improvement opportunity.

Before Analyze starts, the Measure-phase maps get one final pass.

Add to each step:
- Process time (in minutes)
- Lag time (in minutes or hours)
- Classification (VA, BVA, NVA)
- Defect rate where applicable

The result is a process map that doesn't just show the steps — it shows the cost of each step in time and quality. This is what the Analyze phase will work from.

Activity 5.08 closes the Measure phase by listing every input and output for each sub-process activity.

Why this matters: the next phase (Analyze) will rank these inputs by impact. You can't rank what isn't listed.

A typical activity has 5-15 inputs. By the time you're done with 5.08, you'll have 50-200 inputs catalogued across the full process. That looks like a lot. The Cause and Effect Matrix in Chapter 6 will tell you which 10-20 actually matter.

The Pareto Principle: ~20% of inputs cause ~80% of outcomes.

Chapter 6 — Analyze — uses two tools to find that critical 20%:

1. Cause and Effect Matrix — ranks all inputs by their correlation to process outputs.
2. FMEA (Failure Modes and Effects Analysis) — deep-dives the top inputs to identify failure modes, root causes, and corrective actions.

By the end of Chapter 6, you'll know exactly which inputs to attack in the Improve phase. The math beats the opinions.

The Cause and Effect Matrix is a spreadsheet. Columns are process outputs (with customer importance scores). Rows are process inputs.

For each cell, score the correlation: 0 (no correlation), 1 (weak), 4 (moderate), 9 (strong).

Multiply correlation by output importance. Sum across rows. Sort descending.

The top 20% of inputs are your candidates for FMEA. The bottom 80% get parked. Done well, this exercise takes 90 minutes and saves the team a week of unfocused analysis.

Three rules for running a Cause and Effect Matrix:

1. Score correlation collectively, not individually. The matrix is a team consensus tool, not a private exercise.

2. Use only 0, 1, 4, 9. No 2s, 5s, 7s. The Fibonacci-like spacing forces clarity.

3. Score every cell. Empty cells signal incomplete thinking.

The output is a ranked list of inputs. The math does the prioritization. Your job is to make sure the inputs are correctly classified.

FMEA gives every failure mode a Risk Priority Number:

RPN = Severity × Occurrence × Detection

Severity (1-10): how bad is the impact when it fails?
Occurrence (1-10): how often does it fail?
Detection (1-10): how likely are we to catch it before customer impact?

Max RPN = 1,000. Anything above 200 gets acted on this Kaizen Event. Anything with Severity 9 or 10 gets acted on regardless of RPN.

Re-score after action. The drop in RPN is your measurable improvement.

FMEA is a structured table. One row per failure mode. For each:

1. Identify the failure mode
2. List the effects
3. Score severity
4. List potential causes
5. Score occurrence
6. List current controls
7. Score detection
8. Calculate RPN
9. Recommend action

The discipline is what makes it work. Skipping steps produces a spreadsheet that looks like an FMEA but isn't one.

Before moving to Improve, the team summarizes the Analyze phase output:

- Top 5-10 critical inputs (from the C&E Matrix)
- Top 5-10 failure modes by RPN (from the FMEA)
- Quick-win recommendations (high RPN, low complexity)
- Long-term recommendations (high RPN, high complexity)

This summary becomes the basis for the Improvement Backlog. Quick wins get implemented during the event. Long-term items get scheduled for follow-on sprints.

Chapter 7 is Improve. Six activities that take the analysis output and turn it into implemented changes — by Friday demo.

This is where most consulting engagements over-promise and under-deliver. They identify 30 improvements, implement zero by Friday, and call it "recommendations for the team to execute."

That's not a Kaizen Event. That's a report. The point of Improve is implemented change, demonstrated, with a control plan, signed off by the sponsor.

Before improvements get planned, the FMEA gets updated with current-state RPNs.

This is the "before" picture. Every prioritized failure mode has a documented RPN, severity score, and current control. When improvements are implemented, the FMEA gets re-scored. The delta is the measurable improvement.

Without this step, you can't quantify the improvement. With it, you can prove $X of risk reduction in audit-ready language.

The Improvement Backlog is the list of changes the team will implement this sprint.

Each backlog item has:
- A clear statement of the improvement
- The failure mode it addresses
- The expected RPN reduction
- The owner (one person)
- The effort estimate (in hours)
- Acceptance criteria (how do we know it's done)

If a backlog item can't articulate all six, it's not a backlog item yet. It's a wish.

Sprint planning takes 90 minutes. The output: a sequenced list of backlog items the team will deliver in the available time.

Sort by:
- Severity score (high severity gets priority)
- Effort vs. RPN reduction (highest impact per hour first)
- Dependencies (some items must precede others)

Don't over-commit. A sprint with eight items and four completed is a failure. A sprint with five items and five completed is a success. Set the team up to win.

The sprint runs Days 3-4 of the event. Twelve hours of focused work, with the facilitator running interference.

Three sprint disciplines:

1. Daily 15-minute standup. What did you finish, what are you working on, what's blocking you?
2. Visible progress board. Backlog items move from To-Do to In-Progress to Done. Everyone sees it.
3. Same-day blocker resolution. If something is blocking, the facilitator unblocks within the hour.

At the end of Day 4, the team reviews what got done.

For each backlog item:
- Is it complete against the acceptance criteria?
- Is the new state documented (updated SOP, new control, new metric)?
- Has the FMEA been re-scored?

Items that aren't complete by Day 4 either get pushed to a follow-on sprint or get descoped from the engagement. Don't pretend incomplete work is complete. The control plan won't survive contact with reality.

The Friday morning retrospective is 30 minutes. Three questions:

1. What worked? (Things to keep doing)
2. What didn't? (Things to stop or change)
3. What did we learn? (Things to remember)

This is the team's last chance to improve the methodology before they apply it to the next process. Capture every insight in the project log.

The retrospective is the Kaizen of the Kaizen. The whole methodology improves itself with each event.

The Appendix of Process Kaizen is the reference section — 11 Lean tools that any practitioner should know cold.

Each is covered in plain English with the same structure: What it is, Why it matters, When to use it, How to do it.

Over the next 12 posts, I'll walk through all 11. Some you'll already know. Some you'll think you know but probably don't. All of them belong in the toolkit.

Standard Work is the documented best-known method for completing a task.

Three components:
1. TAKT time (the customer's pace)
2. Work sequence (the order of operations)
3. Standard in-process inventory (the minimum WIP)

Without Standard Work, every operator does the job differently, and the process drifts. With it, drift becomes visible — and improvement becomes possible.

Standard Work is the foundation of every other Lean improvement.

Training in a Lean organization isn't classroom hours. It's job qualification — measured by performance against the Standard Work.

Four levels of operator capability:
1. Aware (knows the work exists)
2. Trained (has done it under supervision)
3. Qualified (can do it independently)
4. Coach (can train others)

Track the matrix. A cell without a level rating is a risk. A process where most operators are at Level 1 or 2 is a process one absence away from failure.

The Eight Wastes are not just a checklist. They're a daily observation discipline.

Walk the process every week. For each step, ask: which of the eight is present here?

D - Defects
O - Overproduction
W - Waiting
N - Non-utilized talent
T - Transport
I - Inventory
M - Motion
E - Excess processing

The waste doesn't go away because you ran a Kaizen Event. It comes back. The discipline of weekly observation is what keeps it gone.

6S has six steps, executed in order:

Sort — separate the needed from the unneeded
Set in Order — a place for everything, everything in its place
Shine — clean as inspection
Standardize — write down the new normal
Sustain — audit and reinforce
Safety — embed safety considerations at every step

The discipline isn't doing 6S once. It's repeating it monthly, quarterly, annually. Every cycle reveals new waste. Every cycle raises the standard.

SMED — Single-Minute Exchange of Die — is the discipline of reducing setup time on any process.

The core technique: separate internal setup (must be done with the machine stopped) from external setup (can be done while the machine is running).

Then convert as much internal setup to external as possible.

The original Toyota example took machine changeover from 4 hours to 3 minutes. Office equivalent: take onboarding setup from 2 weeks to 2 days. Same principle. Different process.

TPM is preventive maintenance, structured.

Six TPM losses:
1. Equipment breakdowns
2. Setup and changeover
3. Minor stops and idling
4. Reduced speed
5. Defects and rework
6. Startup losses

The goal: maximize Overall Equipment Effectiveness (OEE) = Availability × Performance × Quality.

In an office context, your "equipment" is the systems and tools your team uses daily. The principles transfer directly. Schedule the maintenance. Track the losses.

Visual Controls operate on one principle: information lives at the point of use.

Five Visual Control types:
1. Standards displayed (the expected state)
2. Performance displayed (the current state)
3. Variance displayed (the gap)
4. Action displayed (what to do about the variance)
5. Ownership displayed (who is responsible)

Walk any operational floor. Count how many of the five are visible. The number you find correlates almost perfectly with the maturity of the Lean implementation.

TAKT time = available production time ÷ customer demand.

If you have 420 minutes of usable production time per day and your customer needs 280 units, TAKT = 1.5 minutes.

That means one unit must come off the line every 90 seconds. No faster (overproduction). No slower (missed demand).

TAKT is the pace of customer demand, translated into operator rhythm. It's how Lean keeps production aligned with the actual market — not with internal forecasts.

Most processes start as batches. They evolve through four stages toward continuous flow:

1. Functional batches (work piles up between departments)
2. Process cells (related work grouped together)
3. One-piece flow (single units move through cells)
4. Continuous flow (no waiting, no batching, no inventory between steps)

Each stage halves the inventory and cycle time of the prior stage. The goal isn't to reach stage 4 — most processes can't. The goal is to keep evolving.

Just-in-Time has one rule: produce only what the customer pulls, only when they pull it.

This eliminates inventory, surfaces problems immediately, and tightens the connection between supply and demand.

JIT is easy to admire and hard to implement. It requires reliable upstream suppliers, predictable customer demand, and processes capable of operating at TAKT.

Start by reducing batch sizes incrementally. Each reduction surfaces a new constraint. Solve it. Reduce again.

The Control Plan is the post-Kaizen contract. The single document that determines whether the gains stick or evaporate.

It specifies:
- Which inputs we measure
- What spec they need to hit
- Who measures
- How often
- What we do when they drift

If your consultant didn't hand you a Control Plan at close-out, the engagement wasn't actually done.

This is the difference between a Kaizen Event that holds and one that quietly reverts within six months.

GLOSSARY: Andon Cord

A signal that any operator can pull to stop the process when something is wrong.

The Toyota assembly line was the original. But the principle works in any process: any team member, at any level, can halt the work when they see a defect, a safety issue, or a quality concern.

The cultural test: when someone pulls the cord, what happens? In a Lean culture, the team gathers and solves. In a non-Lean culture, the puller gets reprimanded.

Which culture do you work in?

GLOSSARY: Cause and Effect Analysis

A structured method for identifying the few inputs that drive the most output variation.

The most common tool: the Cause and Effect Matrix (covered in Chapter 6). Inputs in rows, outputs in columns, correlation scores in cells.

The principle is older than the matrix: not all inputs are equal. Twenty percent of them produce eighty percent of the outcome. Find the twenty percent. Stop optimizing the rest.

caption:
GLOSSARY: Cycle Time vs. TAKT Time

Cycle time is how long the process actually takes.
TAKT time is how long it should take, given customer demand.

Three states:
- Cycle time < TAKT: overproduction. You're building inventory.
- Cycle time = TAKT: balanced. You're meeting demand exactly.
- Cycle time > TAKT: you can't keep up. Demand is unmet.

Most operations focus on cycle time alone. The TAKT comparison is what reveals whether the cycle time is right.

GLOSSARY: DMAIC

The Six Sigma project lifecycle. Five phases:

D - Define the problem and the scope
M - Measure the current state
A - Analyze the root causes
I - Improve the process
C - Control the new state

The seven chapters of Process Kaizen map to DMAIC. The methodology isn't novel — it's the disciplined execution that produces results.

Most teams skip Control. That's why most improvements don't stick.

GLOSSARY: Failure Modes and Effects Analysis (FMEA)

A structured method for evaluating risk in a process or product.

For each potential failure mode, score three dimensions:
- Severity (impact when it happens)
- Occurrence (how often it happens)
- Detection (how likely we are to catch it before customer impact)

Multiply: Risk Priority Number (RPN). Sort. Act on the highest.

FMEA turns risk from a feeling into a number. Numbers are debatable. Feelings aren't.

GLOSSARY: Five Whys

The root cause analysis technique that asks "why" five times.

Problem: shipment late.
Why? Truck wasn't loaded on time.
Why? Order wasn't picked on time.
Why? System didn't release the pick list.
Why? Approval was pending.
Why? Approver was unavailable, no backup process.

Root cause: missing backup approver protocol. Five questions to get from symptom to fix.

The technique looks simple. Practicing it is harder than it looks. Most people stop at why-2.

GLOSSARY: Just-in-Time (JIT)

A production philosophy: make only what is demanded, only when it's demanded.

JIT eliminates inventory, surfaces problems immediately, and aligns supply with actual customer demand rather than forecasts.

Three preconditions for JIT to work:
1. Reliable upstream suppliers
2. Predictable customer demand
3. Capable processes at TAKT

JIT is admired everywhere and implemented well in few places. It requires Lean maturity that takes years to build. Start by reducing batch sizes.

GLOSSARY: Kanban

A signal — usually a card — that triggers production or replenishment.

The original Toyota Kanban was a paper card that an operator pulled from a parts bin when the bin was empty. The card went back to the supplier, who refilled the bin and returned the card.

Modern Kanban can be a card, a digital signal, an empty bin, a colored light. The form doesn't matter. The principle does: nothing gets produced without a pull signal from downstream.

GLOSSARY: The Pareto Principle (80/20 Rule)

Roughly 20% of inputs cause 80% of outputs. In any process, the Pareto Principle holds with surprising regularity.

20% of customers generate 80% of revenue.
20% of defects cause 80% of returns.
20% of process steps consume 80% of cycle time.

The Pareto Principle is the conceptual basis for the Cause and Effect Matrix. Find the 20% that matters. Stop spending effort on the 80% that doesn't.

GLOSSARY: Poka-Yoke (Mistake Proofing)

Designing the process so a mistake is impossible.

Examples:
- USB-C: works in either orientation. Earlier USB only worked one way and people fumbled.
- A car that won't start unless the brake is depressed.
- A form field that won't accept a date in the past for future appointments.

Poka-Yoke is the highest form of process control. The defect can't occur because the design prevents it. Cheaper than inspection. More reliable than training.

GLOSSARY: Pull System

A production system where work is initiated only by downstream demand signals.

Push: "We made it, here it is, deal with it."
Pull: "You asked for it, so we made it."

Pull systems reduce inventory, expose problems immediately, and align production with actual customer demand. They require reliable processes and short cycle times to work.

Most organizations operate on push and call it pull. The test: do you produce anything without a confirmed customer order?

GLOSSARY: SIPOC

Five columns that frame any process:

Suppliers · Inputs · Process · Outputs · Customers

Used at the start of Define (Chapter 4) to establish shared understanding. Takes 45 minutes. Reveals process boundaries, key handoffs, and assumptions the team didn't know they were making.

Most teams skip SIPOC because it looks too simple. Most teams that skip SIPOC end up rebuilding their process map on Day 3 of the event.

GLOSSARY: Six Sigma

A methodology for reducing variation in any process.

The name comes from statistics: six standard deviations between the process mean and the nearest spec limit, which corresponds to 3.4 defects per million opportunities.

In practice, Six Sigma is the DMAIC project methodology, applied to processes where variation drives quality issues. Combined with Lean (which reduces waste), the combined practice is Lean Six Sigma.

GLOSSARY: Standard Work

The documented best-known method for completing a task.

Standard Work has three components:
- TAKT time (the customer's required pace)
- Work sequence (the order of operations)
- Standard work-in-process (the minimum WIP)

The point of Standard Work isn't to lock in the current state. It's to make the current state visible — so improvements can be made deliberately, documented, and rolled out across the team.

Without Standard Work, every improvement is private.

GLOSSARY: TAKT Time

The rate at which customer demand must be filled.

TAKT = Available Production Time ÷ Customer Demand

If you have 480 minutes per day and 240 units of demand, TAKT = 2 minutes per unit.

TAKT is the rhythm Lean operations align to. Below TAKT and you overproduce. Above TAKT and you miss demand. Matching TAKT — consistently — is the operational goal.

GLOSSARY: Value Stream

The complete sequence of activities required to bring a product or service from order to delivery.

Value Stream Mapping (VSM) is the discipline of mapping this end-to-end, including:
- Process steps
- Inventory and WIP at each step
- Cycle times
- Lag times
- Information flows

A VSM shows the whole system. A process map shows a piece of it. Most improvements happen at the system level — between steps, not within them.
